analysis.title: Chipping in: how chips have become a huge driver of the dollar
key_insights: DB argues the petrodollar is being superseded by a 'chip-dollar': global trade in semiconductors now exceeds trade in oil and gas for the first time (four quarters of exports to Q2-2026), and Asia ex-China chip surpluses are as large as the Gulf's petroleum-related surpluses.

Asian chip surpluses are being recycled into US equities, not US Treasuries as petrodollar surpluses were. Foreign purchases of US equities have exceeded USD1tn over the past year and are more than double foreign Treasury allocations. Most of the increase has come from Asia.

Korea is the template: semiconductor exports are up over 200% YoY this year, the chip trade surplus is close to USD250bn, and chips account for 100% of Korea's overall trade surplus. Foreign sales of Korean equities and Korean purchases of overseas equities each account for half of the past year's capital outflows.

The US accounts for about 50% of global equity market capitalization but 70% of Korea's overseas equity holdings, and over 90% of Korean households' foreign equity exposure. Japanese retail is allocating to US-focused ETFs via NISA, and US asset tokenization and 23/5 trading could extend the trend.

Chips play the role in the digital economy that oil played in the industrial one. Servers are about 60% of the annualized cost of an indicative 1GW US data centre (Epoch AI), chips are 95% of an AI server rack's value (SIA), so chips are over 50% of AI data centre capex. Bloomberg Intelligence puts hyperscaler capex commitments near USD8tn to 2031, implying about USD4tn of chip demand.

US control over chips rests on technology and rents: about 50% of supply-chain value is in design, where US firms hold 87% of revenue. The US has a near monopoly on EDA software and about 60% of manufacturing equipment revenue, and 70% of industry profits flow to US firms (Starrs). Key producers in Japan, Taiwan and Korea are US-aligned, which DB calls a US-Asia chip-dollar bloc.

China runs a large semiconductor deficit despite a manufactured goods surplus above USD2tn. Under 20% of the net international assets of China are in portfolio investments versus nearly 50% for Korea, Japan and Taiwan, and China shows a growing preference for gold over dollar assets.

There is circularity: US AI equity financing is funded by Asian chip surpluses that are themselves boosted by US AI demand. If demand for compute disappoints, earnings estimates and chip demand fall together, challenging foreign equity financing of the US from both push and pull sides. Chinese open-source models could also hurt US company profitability.

Because dollar support now depends on equity rather than Treasury inflows, DB expects higher USD volatility over time. Realized S&P 500 volatility is about 3x that of the US 10Y, Nasdaq is double the S&P, and the Philly Semiconductor Index more than triple.
DB will release updated medium-term FX forecasts later this week reflecting these dynamics.

sector_views.rationale: Chips are now the largest traded commodity-like input and the main driver of Asian surpluses and AI capex, with about USD4tn of further chip demand implied by hyperscaler capex plans to 2031.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Memory chip demand for AI is driving Korea's trade surplus and capital outflows into US equities.
Equals 100% of Korea's overall trade surplus.
More than double foreign Treasury purchases, now the mainstay of US deficit funding.
Bloomberg Intelligence estimate, implying about USD4tn of chip demand.

crypto_views: The US embrace of asset tokenization is cited as a factor that could enable more retail access to US equities.
risk_factors: AI data centre buildout may slow due to US political climate, calls for public oversight and safety monitoring, or tighter export controls.
Chip demand may be one-off during capacity buildout rather than ongoing like oil, though chip replacement cycles of 3-7 years suggest some ongoing demand.
Circularity: weaker consumer demand for compute would cut AI earnings estimates and chip demand, hurting foreign equity financing of the US.
Chinese open-source AI models could undermine US company profitability and the attractiveness of US markets to global capital.
Greater reliance on equity inflows makes the dollar more volatile and exposed.
charts_described: Figure 1: global trade in chips has overtaken trade in oil and gas for the first time in history.
Figure 2: Asia ex-China chip surpluses are now as large as the Gulf's petroleum-related surpluses.
Figure 3: Korea's chip surplus is recycled into equities, with foreign sales of Korean equities and Korean purchases of overseas equities each about half of capital outflows.
Figure 5: foreign flows into US stocks exceed flows into US Treasuries by a significant margin.
vol_and_positioning: Realized volatility of the S&P 500 is about 3 times that of the US 10Y Treasury, Nasdaq volatility is double the S&P, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is more than triple the S&P.
DB expects higher USD volatility over time as dollar support shifts from Treasury to equity inflows.
geopolitical: The Iran war could undermine the petrodollar system by challenging the US security umbrella and perceptions of US geopolitical leadership.

US export controls on chips to China, with USTR Greer saying the US wants the 'crown jewels' of semiconductors kept with the US or allies, and possible tightening on leasing of data centres built with US chips to non-US allies.
US-China technology race, with China restricted from EUV lithography while pursuing self-sufficiency.
China's reserve preference is shifting toward gold over dollar assets.

tension_points.bull_case: Asian chip surpluses recycled into US equities and corporate bonds fund the US deficit and the AI buildout, with US control of design, EDA and equipment and US-aligned Asian producers sustaining the flows; chip replacement cycles of 3-7 years suggest ongoing demand.
tension_points.bear_case: Circularity: flows are funded by surpluses boosted by US AI demand, so weaker compute demand would cut earnings estimates and chip demand together. Equities are far more volatile than Treasuries, so the dollar becomes more volatile, and Chinese open-source models could hurt US profitability.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Consumer demand for compute failing to keep up with costly supply investment, which would reduce AI earnings estimates and chip demand.

theme_stances.key_argument: Chip surpluses in Asia recycled into US equities are replacing petrodollar Treasury recycling as the foundation of dollar dominance.
theme_stances.evidence: the petrodollar is – rather quickly - being superseded by the chip-dollar

theme_stances.key_argument: Dependence on foreign equity inflows rather than Treasury inflows should spill over into higher US dollar volatility over time.
theme_stances.evidence: should spill over into currency volatility in time
